newsitem.title: USA: Fed knocks down some bank-securities "firewalls".
newsitem.headline: Fed knocks down some bank-securities "firewalls".

text.p: The Federal Reserve Board Wednesday knocked down some barriers between banks and their securities affiliates, which bankers saw as a step toward allowing one-stop shopping for consumers of various financial products.
The Fed loosened three "firewalls" designed to keep banks at arm's length from their securities subsidiaries.

Now banks will be able to share employees with a securities affiliate and market the products of a securities subsidiary. The Fed also eased restrictions on banks that buy and sell securities for their own portfolios via securities affiliates.
"The Fed has taken one more step to allow banks to act more like securities firms," said Larry LaRocco, managing director of the American Bankers Association's securities association.
"It simply means that your banker will now have access to more securities products, have a wider array of financial products for (customers)," he added.
Thirty-nine bank holding companies have securities subsidiaries, known as "section 20" subsidiaries after the section of the Glass-Steagall Act that allowed their creation.
The Depression-era Glass-Steagall law separates commercial and investment banking.
The Fed is still considering a key proposal that would expand the allowable activity of section 20 subsidiaries in securities like stocks, corporate bonds and municipal bonds.
That proposal would allow a securities subsidiary to derive as much as 25 percent of its total revenue from those activities, up from the current 10 percent limit.
The comment period for that proposal ended Sept. 30. Bankers estimated the Fed may take it up next month.
Congressional efforts to dismantle the Glass-Steagall law fell short earlier this year even as Fed officials continued to call for its repeal.
"I hope we get rid of the legislation, but absent that, this is a very good (proposal)," Fed Governor Susan Phillips said at the meeting Wednesday.
The Fed's action would result in cost savings for banks and may encourage more banks to seek securities affiliates, banking groups said.

While the Fed's move would eliminate the need for costly hiring of personnel with overlapping expertise, a bank's chief executive officer would still be prohibited from occupying that position at its securities affiliate
Also, bank directors and officers would not be allowed to hold a majority of board seats at the securities subsidiary, the Fed said.
The Fed's repeal of "cross-marketing" restrictions would allow a bank to market the products of the securities subsidiary.

"I think probably the biggest dividend of this will be to the customer who will now be able to deal with one person ... or at least a team ... that can meet the customer's needs through an array of products," said Richard Whiting, general counsel for The Bankers Roundtable.
